lessons.title: Moments, support reactions and composite rods
lessons.summary: Balance turning effects as well as forces, with every weight at its own centre.
lessons.objective: Use moments and mass-weighted coordinates to determine support forces and centres of mass.
lessons.before: Review resolving forces, simultaneous equations and signed components. Distinguish mass from weight. A rigid body has fixed shape; static equilibrium also requires no net turning effect.
lessons.ideas:
A moment uses a perpendicular distance

The moment of a force about a point measures its turning effect. Its magnitude is force times the perpendicular distance to its line of action. Choose one sign convention; below, anticlockwise is positive. With position relative to the chosen point and coplanar force components,

\[\begin{gathered}M=xF_y-yF_x\end{gathered}\]

This formula follows by adding the moments of the horizontal and vertical components. A force through the chosen point has zero moment. The length of a sloping rod is not automatically the lever arm. Moments have units N m; they are signed, unlike their magnitudes.

Three equations for a planar rigid body

\[\begin{gathered}\sum F_x=0,\qquad\sum F_y=0,\qquad\sum M_O=0\end{gathered}\]

Choose a moment point that removes unknown forces when possible. Force balance alone can leave a couple, and zero moment alone need not give zero resultant force. A hinge can exert horizontal and vertical components. A smooth contact supplies only a normal reaction; it cannot pull a body back onto the support.

Replace distributed weight at the centre of mass

A uniform straight rod has its centre at its midpoint. For separated components with masses and known centres, matching first moments gives

\[\begin{gathered}\bar x=\frac{\sum m_i x_i}{\sum m_i},\qquad \bar y=\frac{\sum m_i y_i}{\sum m_i}\end{gathered}\]

Use masses, not merely lengths, unless all rods have the same mass per unit length. A light connector contributes no weight. Discs and spheres in a frame act at their own centres. A centre of mass can lie in an empty region of a frame.

Test the support conditions

After solving the equilibrium equations, check every one-sided reaction is non-negative. At a loss-of-contact threshold it can be zero. A negative result means the assumed contact is not physically possible; it is not a downward force from an ordinary support. Hinges are different because they can sustain either sign of component.

Suspension of a composite frame

In freely hanging equilibrium the centre of mass is vertically below the suspension point. Find its position in body-fixed axes first, then compare the suspension-to-centre line with the named side. Do not interchange an angle to the horizontal with its complementary angle.
lessons.method:
1. List the bodies and all external forces with their points of action.
  2. Take signed moments about a useful point and resolve forces in two directions.
  3. For composite bodies, use the actual component masses and centres.
  4. Solve for all requested force components or coordinates.
  5. Check force signs, unilateral contacts, units and any parameter restrictions.
mistakes: Use perpendicular distance, not the distance along the rod, for a moment.
Zero resultant force does not by itself remove a turning couple.
A hinge reaction need not be perpendicular to the rod.
Equal lengths need not mean equal masses when linear densities differ.
A negative normal reaction invalidates a one-sided-contact assumption.

examples.title: 1 · The sign changes with the moment point
examples.question: A force \((4,5)\) N acts at \((3,2)\) m. Find its signed moment about the origin and about \(P=(1,-1)\), using anticlockwise positive.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}M_O=3(5)-2(4)=7\\\boldsymbol r_P=(2,3)\\M_P=2(5)-3(4)=-2\end{gathered}\]

The first moment is 7 N m anticlockwise; the second has magnitude 2 N m clockwise. The force is unchanged, but its lever arm relative to the selected point changes.

examples.title: 2 · Both reactions of a loaded beam
examples.question: A uniform horizontal beam of length 5 m and weight 40 N rests on smooth supports at its ends. A 30 N load is attached 4 m from the left end. Find both upward reactions.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}5R_B=40\left(\frac52\right)+30(4)\\R_B=44,\qquad R_A+R_B=70\\R_A=26\end{gathered}\]

Both reactions are positive, so the assumed contacts are possible. Their sum balances the full 70 N load, not only the beam weight.

examples.title: 3 · A bracket with unequal linear densities
examples.question: Two uniform rods join at right angles: a horizontal rod from \((0,0)\) to \((4,0)\) has mass 2 kg, and a vertical rod to \((4,3)\) has mass 3 kg. Find the combined centre. If suspended from the origin, find the tangent of the acute angle between the originally horizontal rod and the downward vertical.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G_1=(2,0),\qquad G_2=\left(4,\frac32\right)\\\bar x=\frac{2(2)+3(4)}5=\frac{16}5\\\bar y=\frac{3(3/2)}5=\frac9{10}\\\tan\phi=\frac{\bar y}{\bar x}=\frac9{32}\end{gathered}\]

The rods have different mass per unit length, so weighting by length would be incorrect. In the hanging configuration the line from the origin to the combined centre points vertically down.

examples.title: 4 · A cable and a two-component hinge force
examples.question: A horizontal rod of length 4 m and weight 60 N is hinged at \(A=(0,0)\). A cable joins \(B=(4,0)\) to \(D=(0,3)\). A 20 N load is fixed 3 m from A. Find the cable tension and both hinge components.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}4\left(\frac35T\right)=60(2)+20(3)\\T=75\\H=\frac45T=60\\V=80-\frac35T=35\end{gathered}\]

The hinge acts rightwards and upwards. Taking moments about A removed its force from that equation; it did not imply that the hinge force was zero.

lessons.title: Plane laminas, suspension and toppling
lessons.summary: Use signed areas for the centre, then test its line of weight against the support.
lessons.objective: Find centres of composite laminas and complete equilibrium ranges for suspension, tilting and cut shapes.
lessons.before: Complete moments and weighted centres. Review quadratic inequalities. Uniform lamina means constant mass per unit area, not necessarily equal masses for unequal pieces.
lessons.ideas:
Areas can stand in for masses only under a common density

A rectangle has its centre at its geometric centre; a uniform triangle has the average of its three vertex coordinates. For a composite uniform lamina, replace mass by area in the first-moment equations. A removed piece contributes negative area and negative first moment.

\[\begin{gathered}\bar x=\frac{A_0x_0-A_hx_h}{A_0-A_h}\\\bar y=\frac{A_0y_0-A_hy_h}{A_0-A_h}\end{gathered}\]

Choose disjoint pieces, or explicitly subtract overlaps. Keep the remaining area positive. A similar planar piece scaled by \(q\) has area scaled by \(q^2\), not \(q\). For a wire frame use line masses instead of filled-in areas.

A named angle requires the correct reference line

When suspended from \(S\), the vector from S to the centre of mass becomes vertically downward. The angle between a body side and the vertical is therefore the angle between that side and the S-to-centre line in the original diagram. Use the correct opposite and adjacent distances, including their signs when deciding the orientation.

Toppling is a support-boundary condition

On a horizontal supporting segment, the vertical projection of the centre must lie within the segment. At an endpoint the object is in limiting equilibrium. If a corner has been removed, the surviving base may be shorter than the original width.

Tilting changes the projection, not the body-fixed centre

Let the base run from downhill coordinate \(0\) to uphill coordinate \(b\), and let the centre have body-fixed coordinates \((\bar x,\bar y)\), with \(\bar y>0\). If the base rises to the right at angle \(\alpha\), the weight line intersects it at

\[\begin{gathered}s=\bar x-\bar y\tan\alpha\\0\le s\le b\end{gathered}\]

At downhill toppling, \(\tan\alpha_T=\bar x/\bar y\). A different supporting edge or tilt direction changes the geometry. Do not use a radius or half-width without identifying the actual pivot.

Sliding can happen before toppling

When weight and the plane contact are the only external forces, the required friction-to-normal ratio is \(\tan\alpha\). Thus no sliding requires \(\tan\alpha\le\mu\). Compare this threshold with the toppling threshold. Saying “friction is sufficient” is an assumption; otherwise check it.
lessons.method:
1. Select body-fixed axes and disjoint positive and removed pieces.
  2. Calculate both first moments using area or the actual masses.
  3. For hanging, compare the suspension-to-centre line with the named side.
  4. For standing or tilting, locate the weight-line projection on the actual base.
  5. Intersect geometric, positivity, friction and endpoint conditions.
mistakes: A hole subtracts both mass and first moment.
The centre of a triangle is not generally halfway up its height.
The suspension angle to one side may be complementary to another named angle.
Toppling depends on the surviving support, not the outline before cutting.
Check sliding separately before claiming that a toppling threshold is reached.

examples.title: 1 · An off-centre rectangular hole
examples.question: A uniform \(6\) cm by \(4\) cm rectangle occupies \(0\le x\le6,\ 0\le y\le4\). A \(2\) cm by \(2\) cm rectangle centred at \((4,2)\) is removed. Find the remaining centre of mass.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}A=24-4=20\\20\bar x=24(3)-4(4)=56\\20\bar y=24(2)-4(2)=40\\G=\left(\frac{14}5,2\right)\end{gathered}\]

The hole is to the right of the original centre, so the remaining centre moves left. The horizontal symmetry through y=2 is preserved.

examples.title: 2 · Read the suspension angle from the geometry
examples.question: A uniform lamina is formed from the triangle with vertices \((0,0),(6,0),(6,3)\) and the rectangle \(6\le x\le8,\ 0\le y\le3\). It is held rigidly as one body and suspended from \(S=(0,3)\). Find its centre and the tangent of the angle between the originally downward side from S to the origin and the downward vertical.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}A_1=9,\quad G_1=(4,1)\\A_2=6,\quad G_2=\left(7,\frac32\right)\\\bar x=\frac{9(4)+6(7)}{15}=\frac{26}5\\\bar y=\frac{9(1)+6(3/2)}{15}=\frac65\\G=\left(\frac{26}5,\frac65\right)\\\tan\phi=\frac{26/5}{3-6/5}=\frac{26}9\end{gathered}\]

The two pieces share their vertical joining edge. The vertical separation is measured from S, not from the original horizontal axis.

examples.title: 3 · Compare sliding with toppling
examples.question: A uniform rectangular frame of mass m has a base from \((0,0)\) to \((4,0)\) and centre \((2,3)\). A particle of mass \(\frac m2\) is fixed at \((4,3)\). The base is tilted upwards to the right, with friction coefficient \(\frac12\). Which limit is reached first?
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\bar x=\frac{2+4/2}{1+1/2}=\frac83,\qquad\bar y=3\\\tan\alpha_T=\frac{8}{9}\\\tan\alpha_S=\frac12\lt\frac89\end{gathered}\]

Sliding occurs first. The toppling calculation assumed contact could hold without sliding; the stated friction is not enough to reach that inclination.

examples.title: 4 · A complete range after a corner is cut away
examples.question: From a uniform square \(0\le x,y\le6\), remove the triangle with vertices \((0,0),(h,0),(0,6)\), where \(0\lt h\lt6\). The remainder stands on the surviving bottom segment \(h\le x\le6\). Find the complete allowed h-range, including limiting equilibrium.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}A=36-3h\\\bar x=\frac{108-h^2}{36-3h}\\\bar x\ge h\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h^2-18h+54\ge0\\h=9\pm3\sqrt3\\0\lt h\le9-3\sqrt3\end{gathered}\]

The upper condition \(\bar x\le6\) holds throughout the original geometric domain: \(h^2-18h+108\gt0\). The smaller boundary is where the weight line reaches the newly cut base endpoint.

lessons.title: Composite solids, cavities and shells
lessons.summary: Use volumes or surface areas consistently, and measure every centre from one reference.
lessons.objective: Calculate centres of three-dimensional bodies and apply the correct suspension or toppling geometry.
lessons.before: Complete signed first moments and toppling. Review volumes, surface areas and similarity. Standard cone and hemisphere centre formulas may be used when stated; deriving them by integration is not required here.
lessons.ideas:
Use the right physical measure

For uniform solids of the same density, masses are proportional to volumes. For thin uniform shells of the same surface density, masses are proportional to material surface areas. An axial drawing shows geometry; its areas are not the masses of the three-dimensional components. Different densities must remain as factors.

Standard centres and a common axial coordinate

For a uniform cylinder the centre is halfway along its height. A solid cone of height h has its centre h/4 from the base, or 3h/4 from the vertex. A solid hemisphere of radius R has its centre 3R/8 from its plane face; a thin hemispherical shell has its centre R/2 from that face. These refer to different physical objects.

\[\begin{gathered}\bar z=\frac{\sum m_i z_i}{\sum m_i}\end{gathered}\]

Convert every quoted distance to the same origin and direction before combining it. A cone added above a cylinder has its centre above their joining plane, not above the cylinder's lower base by h/4 alone.

Cavities and frusta

A cavity subtracts mass and its own first moment. A blind bore has the centre of the removed cylinder at half its depth from the opening. A frustum can be treated as a larger cone minus a smaller similar cone. Use the cube of the linear scale factor for the solid-cone mass ratio.

Count the shell surfaces actually present

List lateral surfaces and each included end face separately. A circular joining face contributes mass only if the question retains it. A hemisphere's curved shell area is not its solid volume. The shell examples below state whether a hidden joining face exists.

Equilibrium requires the right geometric projection

For an axisymmetric body with centre height d above a circular base of radius R on a rough incline, downhill toppling occurs at \(d\tan\alpha=R\). Friction must also prevent sliding. When hanging from a rim point, use the centre's signed distance from the plane containing that rim. A curved contact can require a vertical through the contact point instead; the circular-base rule is not universal.
lessons.method:
1. List real material components and removed regions with their density factors.
  2. Choose one reference plane and write every component centre in that coordinate.
  3. Use volume for solids and material area for shells.
  4. Apply signed first moments and verify the remaining mass is positive.
  5. Use the actual suspension point or support geometry and retain every admissible parameter root.
mistakes: An axial cross-sectional area does not weight the masses of solid components.
A cone centre quoted from the vertex differs from the one quoted from its base.
A blind bore is not a hole through the full height.
A closed cylinder has end faces; an open joining rim does not create a new face.
A real algebraic root must still satisfy cavity-fit and geometric conditions.

examples.title: 1 · A cone above a cylinder
examples.question: A solid cylinder of radius 2 cm and height 6 cm carries a coaxial solid cone of the same radius and height 3 cm. Both have the same density. Use the cone centre at one quarter of its height above its base. Find the combined centre height and the toppling inclination on a sufficiently rough plane.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}V_{\rm cyl}=24\pi,\quad z_{\rm cyl}=3\\V_{\rm cone}=4\pi,\quad z_{\rm cone}=6+\frac34=\frac{27}4\\\bar z=\frac{24(3)+4(27/4)}{28}=\frac{99}{28}\\\tan\alpha_T=\frac2{\bar z}=\frac{56}{99}\end{gathered}\]

The common density and π cancel. The cone centre must include the height of the cylinder underneath it.

examples.title: 2 · A blind bore measured from the top
examples.question: A cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 8 cm has a coaxial blind cylindrical bore of radius 1 cm and depth 4 cm, opening at the top. Find the remaining centre height above the base and its distance below the top.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}V_0=72\pi,\quad z_0=4\\V_h=4\pi,\quad z_h=8-\frac42=6\\\bar z=\frac{72(4)-4(6)}{68}=\frac{66}{17}\\d=8-\bar z=\frac{70}{17}\end{gathered}\]

The removed material is above the original centre, so the remaining centre moves down. Its distance below the top consequently increases.

examples.title: 3 · A frustum from two similar cones
examples.question: A uniform solid frustum has lower radius \(3r\), upper radius r and height h. Find its centre height from the lower face. If \(h=\frac{13r}3\) and it hangs from a lower rim point, find the tangent of the angle between a base diameter through that point and the downward vertical.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}H_{\rm large}=\frac32h,\qquad H_{\rm small}=\frac12h\\m_{\rm large}:m_{\rm small}=27:1\\z_{\rm large}=\frac38h,\qquad z_{\rm small}=h+\frac18h\\\bar z=\frac{27(3h/8)-9h/8}{26}=\frac9{26}h\\\tan\phi=\frac{\bar z}{3r}=\frac12\end{gathered}\]

The subtracted cone centre is measured from the lower face too. In the suspension calculation the horizontal offset is a radius, not a diameter.

examples.title: 4 · An open joining rim is not an extra disc
examples.question: A thin cylindrical shell of radius a and height h has a lower circular face but no top face. A thin hemispherical cap of radius a joins its top rim; there is no internal circular face. All surfaces have the same mass per unit area. Use the cap centre a/2 above its plane face. Find the combined centre and the h-range for equilibrium on a rough incline with \(\tan\alpha=\frac12\), assuming sliding is prevented.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}A_{\rm side}=2\pi ah,\quad A_{\rm bottom}=\pi a^2\\A_{\rm cap}=2\pi a^2\\\bar z=\frac{ah^2+2a^2h+a^3}{2ah+3a^2}\\\bar z=\frac{(h+a)^2}{2h+3a}\\\frac12\bar z\le a\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h^2-2ah-5a^2\le0\\0\lt h\le(1+\sqrt6)a\end{gathered}\]

The top rim has no circular disc, so adding one would change both total mass and first moment. The upper endpoint is included because limiting toppling is allowed.

lessons.title: Contact forces, friction and linked constraints
lessons.summary: Find the required forces before imposing friction limits or an elastic-string law.
lessons.objective: Construct complete force-and-moment models and check all contact, friction and extension conditions.
lessons.before: Complete moments and reactions and centres and toppling. Three written applications also use Hooke’s law, a later-topic prerequisite stated below. No dynamics of rotation or moment of inertia is needed in this chapter.
lessons.ideas:
Draw a separate force at every contact

A smooth plane supplies a force perpendicular to its surface. A smooth peg against a straight rod pushes perpendicular to the rod. A smooth circular surface pushes along its contact normal, through the circle centre. A hinge can have two components; a taut string pulls along its own length. Use the actual geometry to determine these directions.

Friction is an inequality except at a specified limit

\[\begin{gathered}|F|\le\mu N,\qquad N\ge0\end{gathered}\]

The sign of F comes from the tendency to slip or from the equilibrium equations. In limiting equilibrium, use equality with the specified impending-motion direction. At two rough contacts, each friction force has its own normal and coefficient; do not mix the two ratios. A coefficient need not be less than one unless the question says so.

Moments, then force balance, then physical checks

Choose a moment point that removes as many unknown reactions as possible. Resolve forces in convenient perpendicular directions and solve. Only after that compare the required friction with its allowed maximum, check normals are non-negative, and ensure a contact point lies on the actual rod or segment. Do not assume that friction always acts towards a wall.

When a string is elastic

For a light elastic string of natural length \(\ell_0\), extended length \(\ell>\ell_0\) and modulus \(\lambda\),

\[\begin{gathered}T=\lambda\frac{\ell-\ell_0}{\ell_0}\end{gathered}\]

Determine the equilibrium tension from moments and force balance, then use the actual extension in Hooke's law. Modulus has units of force. A string cannot provide compressive tension. With a rough ring, analyse the ring separately as well as the attached rod; their external forces are not identical.

Curved bodies still need moment balance

At a circular contact the normal passes through the centre, so its moment about the centre is zero. Tangential friction and a string attached elsewhere can still have nonzero moments. A horizontal pulling force does not automatically act through the centre. Check all signed lever arms before resolving parallel and perpendicular to an incline.

Compare all possible failure boundaries

A mathematically solved force system may still require a negative normal, a slack string or excessive friction. A contact can be lost before another friction limit is reached. Report the whole allowed parameter interval by intersecting every relevant condition.
lessons.method:
1. Identify each contact normal, friction direction, hinge component and string force.
  2. Write moment and force equations for the chosen body; separate connected bodies when needed.
  3. Apply limiting friction only where the problem specifies the limit.
  4. Use Hooke’s law only after finding the tension and actual extension.
  5. Check all normals, friction bounds, geometry and parameter domains.
mistakes: A smooth peg reaction is perpendicular to the contacting rod, not necessarily vertical.
Friction is not automatically at its maximum in ordinary equilibrium.
Each contact has its own normal reaction in the friction ratio.
Use extension divided by natural length, not total string length, in Hooke’s law.
A force through one moment point can still affect the force-balance equations.

examples.title: 1 · A smooth wall and a rough floor
examples.question: A uniform ladder of weight 100 N rests against a smooth vertical wall. Its inclination has \(\tan\theta=\frac34\). Find the wall reaction, floor normal, required friction and least floor coefficient.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}R_B(L\sin\theta)=100\left(\frac L2\cos\theta\right)\\R_B=\frac{100}{2\tan\theta}=\frac{200}3\\N=100,\quad F=\frac{200}3,\quad\mu_{\min}=\frac23\end{gathered}\]

The wall pushes away from itself, so floor friction acts towards it in this particular configuration. Equality in the friction law describes the least possible coefficient, not every equilibrium coefficient.

examples.title: 2 · A peg gives a different friction direction
examples.question: A uniform rod of length \(5a\) and weight W rises to the right with \(\tan\theta=\frac43\). Its lower end rests on rough horizontal ground. A smooth peg at distance \(3a\) along the rod pushes perpendicular to it, upwards-left. Find the peg reaction, floor normal, friction and least coefficient.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}3aR=W\left(\frac{5a}{2}\right)\frac35,\qquad R=\frac W2\\F=\frac45R=\frac25W\quad\text{rightwards}\\N=W-\frac35R=\frac7{10}W\\\mu_{\min}=\frac FN=\frac47\end{gathered}\]

The peg has a leftward component, so the floor friction here acts rightwards. All normal reactions are positive.

examples.title: 3 · Equilibrium tension before the elastic law
examples.question: A horizontal rod of length \(6a\) and weight W is hinged at its left end. A cable runs from the right end to a wall point \(8a\) above the hinge. A load \(\frac W2\) acts \(4a\) from the hinge. The cable is an elastic string of natural length \(8a\). Find T, both hinge components and its modulus.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}6a\left(\frac45T\right)=3aW+4a\left(\frac W2\right)\\T=\frac{25}{24}W\\H=\frac35T=\frac58W\\V=\frac32W-\frac45T=\frac23W\\\ell=10a,\qquad\lambda=T\frac{8a}{2a}=\frac{25}6W\end{gathered}\]

The current length is obtained from the 6–8–10 triangle. Tension comes from equilibrium; the modulus then follows from the positive extension.

examples.title: 4 · A circular contact still has a friction moment
examples.question: A thin ring of radius a and weight W rests on a rough plane rising rightwards with \(\tan\alpha=\frac34\). A horizontal string pulls rightwards at the point whose radius is parallel to the plane on the upslope side. Find the tension and the coefficient at limiting equilibrium.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\sin\alpha=\frac35,\qquad\cos\alpha=\frac45\\aF=aT\sin\alpha\\T\cos\alpha+F=W\sin\alpha\\T=\frac37W,\quad F=\frac9{35}W\\N=W\cos\alpha+T\sin\alpha=\frac{37}{35}W\\\mu=\frac9{37}\end{gathered}\]

The normal passes through the ring centre, but the friction and off-centre string do not. Friction acts upslope in this configuration; its moment is essential.

questions.prompt_html: A force \(\left( 4, \ 5\right)\) N acts at \(\left( 3, \ 2\right)\) m. Give its signed moment about the origin and about \(\left( 1, \ -1\right)\) m. Anticlockwise is positive.
questions.answer_html: Signed moment about origin: \(7\); Signed moment about specified point: \(-2\)
questions.solution_html:
\[\begin{gathered}M=(x-x_P)F_y-(y-y_P)F_x\end{gathered}\]

Use position relative to each moment point. A negative answer denotes clockwise turning.

questions.title: Both coordinates after removing a hole

questions.title: Cable-supported loading arm
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform horizontal rod \(AB\), of length \(4a\) and weight \(W\), is hinged at \(A\) to a vertical wall. A light cable joins \(B\) to a point \(D\) on the wall, \(3a\) vertically above \(A\). A particle of weight \(W\) is attached at \(C\), where \(AC=3a\). The rod is in equilibrium. Here \(a,W\gt0\).

  1. Find the tension in the cable.

    [3]

  2. Find the horizontal and vertical components of the force exerted by the hinge on the rod.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The cable has length \(5a\); its upward component at \(B\) is \(3T/5\). The rod's weight acts at its midpoint, \(2a\) from \(A\).

Taking moments about \(A\), \[(4a)\frac{3T}{5}=W(2a)+W(3a).\] Thus \(12T/5=5W\), giving \(T=25W/12\).

Part (b)

Horizontal equilibrium gives \(H=4T/5=5W/3\), to the right. Vertical equilibrium gives \(V+3T/5=2W\), hence \(V=3W/4\), upwards. A hinge can supply both components; it is not a smooth wall contact.
questions.hint_html: Take moments about the hinge before resolving the other forces.

questions.title: A cable limit and a hinge condition
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\), of length \(4a\) and mass \(kM\), is rigidly attached at \(B\) to the rim of a uniform disc of radius \(a\) and mass \(3M\). The rod and the diameter through \(B\) form a straight line, with the disc beyond \(B\). The rod is horizontal and hinged at \(A\). A cable joins \(B\) to a point \(3a\) vertically above \(A\). Here \(k\gt0\).

  1. Find the distance of the centre of mass from \(A\).

    [3]

  2. Find the cable tension and the upward component \(V\) of the hinge force.

    [4]

  3. The cable tension must not exceed \(10Mg\), and the hinge force must have no downward vertical component. Find the complete allowed range of \(k\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The component centres are at distances \(2a\) and \(5a\) from \(A\). Therefore \[(k+3)M\bar x=kM(2a)+3M(5a),\] which gives \(\bar x=a(2k+15)/(k+3)\).

Part (b)

The cable has vertical component \(3T/5\). Moments about \(A\) give \[4a\frac{3T}{5}=Mg(2ka+15a).\] Thus \(T=5(2k+15)Mg/12\). Resolving vertically, \[V=(k+3)Mg-\frac35T=\frac{2k-3}{4}Mg.\] A negative value would mean a downward hinge component, not failure of the hinge.

Part (c)

The cable condition is \(5(2k+15)/12\le10\), so \(k\le9/2\). The hinge condition is \(V\ge0\), giving \(k\ge3/2\). Both equalities are allowed. Intersecting these conditions with \(k\gt0\) gives \[\frac32\le k\le\frac92.\]
questions.hint_html: Do not impose a sign restriction on a hinge force unless the question explicitly requires it.

questions.title: Two design limits on a lifting arm
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform horizontal rod \(AB\), length \(6a\) and weight \(2W\), is hinged to a wall at \(A\). A light cable joins \(B\) to a point \(8a\) vertically above \(A\). A particle of weight \(W\) is attached at distance \(xa\) from \(A\), where \(0\le x\le6\).

  1. Find the cable tension in terms of \(x\) and \(W\).

    [4]

  2. Find the horizontal component \(H\) and upward component \(V\) of the hinge reaction.

    [4]

  3. The cable must have \(T\le2W\), while the upward hinge component must have \(V\le3W/2\). Find the complete allowed interval for \(x\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The cable has length \(10a\); its upward component is \(4T/5\). The rod's centre is \(3a\) from \(A\). Taking moments about \(A\), \[6a\frac{4T}{5}=2W(3a)+W(xa).\] Thus \(T=5(6+x)W/24\). It is positive throughout the stated range.

Part (b)

The cable pulls towards the wall with horizontal component \(3T/5\), so the hinge pushes away from the wall with \(H=3T/5=(6+x)W/8\). Vertical equilibrium gives \[V+\frac45T=3W,\qquad V=\frac{12-x}{6}W.\] For \(0\le x\le6\), the stated upward component is positive.

Part (c)

The cable restriction gives \(5(6+x)/24\le2\), hence \(x\le18/5\). The hinge restriction gives \((12-x)/6\le3/2\), hence \(x\ge3\). Their intersection already lies in \([0,6]\), so \[3\le x\le\frac{18}{5}.\] Equality is permitted in both design limits; there is no reason to exclude the endpoints.
questions.hint_html: One limit supplies an upper bound on the load position and the other supplies a lower bound.

questions.title: Balancing a rod and a mounted disc
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\) has length \(8a\) and mass \(M\). A uniform disc of mass \(2M\) and radius \(a\) is rigidly attached with its centre on \(AB\), a distance \(x\) from \(A\), where \(a\le x\le7a\). All weights act in the plane of the assembly.

  1. Find the distance of the centre of mass of the assembly from \(A\).

    [3]

  2. The assembly balances horizontally on a knife edge at distance \(3a\) from \(A\). Find \(x\).

    [2]

  3. Keep this position of the disc and attach a particle of mass \(M\) at \(B\). The horizontal assembly now rests on smooth supports at \(A\) and at \(C\), where \(AC=6a\). Find the reactions and verify that neither support loses contact.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The rod's centre is \(4a\) from \(A\); the disc's centre of mass is its geometric centre. If \(AG=s\), then \[3Ms=M(4a)+2Mx,\] so \(s=(4a+2x)/3\).

Part (b)

With only its weight and the support reaction acting, the centre of mass lies vertically above the knife edge. Thus \((4a+2x)/3=3a\), so \(x=5a/2\), within the specified interval.

Part (c)

The original assembly of mass \(3M\) has its centre at \(3a\). The additional particle is at \(8a\). Taking moments about \(A\), \[6aR_C=3Mg(3a)+Mg(8a)=17Mga.\] Hence \(R_C=17Mg/6\). Vertical equilibrium gives \(R_A=4Mg-R_C=7Mg/6\). Both reactions are positive, so the unilateral supports can supply them.

questions.prompt_html:
Three uniform discs of radius \(a\) are rigidly connected by light rods. Their centres are \(A(0,0)\), \(B(8a,0)\) and \(C(0,6a)\), and their masses are \(2M,M,3M\), respectively. The rods have negligible mass. The discs and rods lie in one plane.

  1. Find the coordinates of the centre of mass.

    [3]

  2. The assembly is suspended freely from \(A\). Find the acute angle between \(AB\) and the downward vertical in equilibrium.

    [3]

  3. A particle of mass \(kM\) is now fixed at \(B\). Find \(k\) so that, when suspended from \(A\), the acute angle between \(AB\) and the downward vertical is \(\tan^{-1}(3/4)\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Symmetry places each disc's centre of mass at its centre. The total mass is \(6M\), so \[\bar x=\frac{M(8a)}{6M}=\frac{4a}{3},\qquad \bar y=\frac{3M(6a)}{6M}=3a.\]

Part (b)

In its hanging position \(AG\) points vertically downwards. The angle between \(AB\) and \(AG\) is unchanged by rotation of the assembly. Hence \[\tan\theta=\frac{3a}{4a/3}=\frac94,\] so \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(9/4)\).

Part (c)

The new centre has coordinates \[\left(\frac{8(1+k)a}{6+k},\frac{18a}{6+k}\right).\] Thus \(\tan\theta=18/[8(1+k)]\). Set this equal to \(3/4\): \(72=24(1+k)\), so \(k=2\). The positive mass and non-zero horizontal coordinate make the chosen acute-angle interpretation valid.
questions.hint_html: The angle is determined by the line from the suspension point to the combined centre of mass.

questions.title: A frame with an eccentric attached mass
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform rectangular lamina has vertices \(A(0,0),B(6a,0),C(6a,4a),D(0,4a)\). A centred rectangle of dimensions \(4a\) by \(2a\), with parallel sides, is removed to make a frame of mass \(m\). A particle of mass \(m/2\) is fixed at \(A\).

  1. Find the centre of mass of the frame and particle together.

    [4]

  2. The assembly hangs in a vertical plane with \(AB\) horizontal, supported by two vertical strings at \(C\) and \(D\). Find the tensions.

    [4]

  3. The string at \(C\) is removed. The assembly is allowed to hang freely from \(D\). Find the acute angle between \(DA\) and the downward vertical.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The frame is symmetric about \(x=3a\) and \(y=2a\), so its centre is \((3a,2a)\). The particle is at the origin and the total mass is \(3m/2\). Thus \[\bar x=\frac{m(3a)}{3m/2}=2a,\qquad \bar y=\frac{m(2a)}{3m/2}=\frac{4a}{3}.\] The mass \(m\) refers to the remaining frame, not the original full rectangle.

Part (b)

Take moments about \(D\). The weight \(3mg/2\) acts a horizontal distance \(2a\) to its right: \[6aT_C=\frac32mg(2a).\] Hence \(T_C=mg/2\). Vertical balance gives \(T_D=3mg/2-T_C=mg\). Both are positive.

Part (c)

Relative to \(D\), the centre of mass is \((2a,-8a/3)\). In the final equilibrium position this displacement points downwards. The angle between the original downward side \(DA\) and this displacement satisfies \[\tan\theta=\frac{2a}{8a/3}=\frac34.\] Therefore \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(3/4)\). No period or moment of inertia is needed.
questions.hint_html: Use the mass of the remaining frame and measure the centre relative to the correct suspension point.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use symmetry and the correct frame mass.

questions.title: Will a ring assembly slide or topple?
questions.prompt_html:
Three thin uniform rings lie in one plane and are rigidly joined at their points of external contact. The upper ring has radius \(a\) and mass \(3M\). The two lower rings each have radius \(2a\) and mass \(2M\), and touch each other. With the lower centres at \((-2a,0)\) and \((2a,0)\), the upper centre lies on the positive \(y\)-axis. The assembly rests with both lower rings touching a plane; its own plane is vertical and contains a line of greatest slope. The coefficient of friction at each contact is \(1/2\).

  1. Find the height of the centre of mass above the plane when it is horizontal.

    [4]

  2. Assuming sufficient friction, find the angle \(\alpha_T\) at which toppling would begin as the supporting plane is tilted.

    [4]

  3. With the stated coefficient of friction, decide whether sliding or toppling occurs first. Justify your comparison.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Each distance from the upper centre to a lower centre is \(3a\). Its height above the line of lower centres is \(\sqrt{(3a)^2-(2a)^2}=\sqrt5a\). The total mass is \(7M\), so the centre of mass is \(3\sqrt5a/7\) above that line. The line is \(2a\) above the supporting plane. Hence \[h=a\left(2+\frac{3\sqrt5}{7}\right).\]

Part (b)

While both lower rings remain in contact, their contact points are \(4a\) apart along the plane. Symmetry puts \(G\) halfway between them, at normal distance \(h\). The vertical line through \(G\) moves downslope by \(h\tan\alpha\). At the toppling threshold it passes through the lower contact, so \[h\tan\alpha_T=2a.\] Substitution gives \(\tan\alpha_T=14/(14+3\sqrt5)\).

Part (c)

Resolving the total external reaction gives total friction \(7Mg\sin\alpha\) and total normal reaction \(7Mg\cos\alpha\). The friction bound is therefore \(\tan\alpha\le1/2\). Before toppling both normal reactions are positive, so this bound can be achieved by assigning the same friction-to-normal ratio at both contacts.

Since \[\frac{14}{14+3\sqrt5}\gt\frac12\] (equivalently \(14\gt3\sqrt5\)), the sliding threshold is smaller. The first loss of equilibrium is sliding at \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}(1/2)\), not toppling.
questions.hint_html: Compare two different thresholds. Do not use the toppling condition before checking friction.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the height of the upper centre.

questions.title: A loaded square wire frame on a slope
questions.prompt_html:
A square wire frame \(ABCD\) has vertices \(A(0,0),B(4a,0),C(4a,4a),D(0,4a)\). Its four uniform rods each have mass \(M\). A square lamina of side \(2a\) and mass \(kM\), where \(k\gt0\), is fixed inside the upper-left corner: its vertices are \((0,2a),(2a,2a),(2a,4a),(0,4a)\). The assembly is placed with \(AB\) along a rough plane rising from \(A\) towards \(B\); the assembly lies in a vertical plane. Sliding is initially prevented.

  1. Find the coordinates of its centre of mass in the given body-fixed axes.

    [5]

  2. The plane is inclined at angle \(\alpha\). Find the condition on \(\alpha\) for equilibrium without toppling, including limiting equilibrium.

    [4]

  3. Toppling begins when \(\tan\alpha=2/3\). Find \(k\).

    [3]

  4. Find the least coefficient of friction that allows this toppling threshold to be reached without earlier sliding.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The four rods have total mass \(4M\) and, by symmetry, centre \((2a,2a)\). The lamina has centre \((a,3a)\). The full mass is \((4+k)M\). Taking first moments in each coordinate gives \[(4+k)M\bar x=8Ma+kMa,\qquad (4+k)M\bar y=8Ma+3kMa.\] Divide by \((4+k)M\) to obtain the stated coordinates.

Part (b)

The vertical projection of \(G\) onto the base, measured from \(A\), is \(p=\bar x-\bar y\tan\alpha\). It must lie between \(0\) and \(4a\). For \(\alpha\ge0\), the upper bound follows from \(\bar x\lt4a\). The lower bound gives \[\tan\alpha\le\frac{\bar x}{\bar y}=\frac{8+k}{8+3k}.\] Equality means incipient toppling about \(A\).

Part (c)

At the threshold, \((8+k)/(8+3k)=2/3\). Hence \(24+3k=16+6k\), so \(k=8/3\). This satisfies the positive-mass restriction.

Part (d)

At inclination \(\alpha\), friction and normal reaction have magnitudes \(W_{\rm total}\sin\alpha\) and \(W_{\rm total}\cos\alpha\). Thus \(\mu\ge\tan\alpha\). The least value at the toppling threshold is \(2/3\); with equality sliding and toppling are simultaneous.
questions.hint_html: Use the projection of the centre of mass onto the inclined base, not its body-fixed horizontal coordinate alone.

marking_criteria.description_html: Set the toppling ratio equal to the given value.

questions.title: A composite beam with two spheres
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\), of length \(4a\) and mass \(\lambda M\), joins two uniform spheres. The left sphere has radius \(a\), mass \(3M\), and centre at coordinate \(-a\) on the line \(AB\), with \(A\) at coordinate zero. The right sphere has radius \(2a\), mass \(4M\), and centre at coordinate \(6a\); \(B\) has coordinate \(4a\). The rod is rigidly attached to each sphere along their line of centres. The assembly rests horizontally on smooth supports at \(A\) and \(B\). Here \(\lambda\gt0\).

  1. Find the position of the combined centre of mass measured from \(A\).

    [4]

  2. Find the support reactions.

    [3]

  3. Given \(R_B=2R_A\), find \(\lambda\).

    [2]

  4. With this value of \(\lambda\), an additional particle of mass \(qM\) is fixed at the centre of the right sphere. Find the largest \(q\) for which both supports can remain in contact.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Symmetry places each sphere's centre of mass at its centre, irrespective of its moment of inertia. The rod centre is \(2a\) from \(A\). Thus \[(7+\lambda)M\bar x=3M(-a)+\lambda M(2a)+4M(6a),\] so \(\bar x=a(21+2\lambda)/(7+\lambda)\). The negative coordinate of the left sphere must be retained.

Part (b)

Taking moments about \(A\), \(4aR_B=(21+2\lambda)Mga\). Therefore \(R_B=(21+2\lambda)Mg/4\). Total vertical balance then gives \(R_A=(7+\lambda)Mg-R_B=(7+2\lambda)Mg/4\). Both are positive for \(\lambda\gt0\).

Part (c)

The reaction ratio gives \(21+2\lambda=2(7+2\lambda)\). Thus \(7=2\lambda\) and \(\lambda=7/2\).

Part (d)

Increasing \(q\) increases the clockwise moment about \(B\). At loss of contact at \(A\), moments about \(B\) give \[3M(5a)+\lambda M(2a)=(4+q)M(2a).\] Thus \(q=(7+2\lambda)/2=7\). For smaller non-negative \(q\), \(R_A\ge0\), while \(R_B\) is positive. Equality is the limiting contact case.
questions.hint_html: Use signed positions along the rod and remember that a smooth support cannot pull downwards.

questions.title: A right-angled wire bracket
questions.prompt_html:
Two uniform rods are rigidly joined at right angles. Rod \(AB\) has length \(6a\) and mass \(3M\); rod \(BC\) has length \(8a\) and mass \(4M\). In body-fixed coordinates, \(A=(0,0),B=(6a,0),C=(6a,8a)\).

  1. Find the centre of mass of the bracket.

    [4]

  2. The bracket hangs freely from \(A\). Find the acute angle between \(AB\) and the downward vertical.

    [3]

  3. A particle of mass \(kM\) is attached at \(C\). Find \(k\) if the new hanging angle is \(45^\circ\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The rod centres are \((3a,0)\) and \((6a,4a)\). The total mass is \(7M\), so \[\bar x=\frac{3M(3a)+4M(6a)}{7M}=\frac{33a}{7},\qquad \bar y=\frac{4M(4a)}{7M}=\frac{16a}{7}.\]

Part (b)

The line \(AG\) is vertical in the hanging position. Its angle to \(AB\) has tangent \(\bar y/\bar x=16/33\). Hence the required acute angle is \(\tan^{-1}(16/33)\).

Part (c)

The new moments are \((33+6k)Ma\) and \((16+8k)Ma\), and both coordinates have denominator \(7+k\). For a \(45^\circ\) hanging angle they must be equal: \[33+6k=16+8k.\] Thus \(k=17/2\). The mass is positive and both centre coordinates are positive, so the intended acute angle is obtained.
questions.hint_html: For a wire bracket, masses are attached to rod midpoints, not to the area enclosed by the rods.

questions.title: A projecting triangular extension
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform lamina is the union of a rectangle with vertices \(O(0,0),A(ka,0),C(ka,3a),D(0,3a)\) and the triangle with vertices \(A,B(ka+h,h),C\). Here \(a,k,h\gt0\). The two regions have the same mass per unit area and meet only along \(AC\). The lamina stands in a vertical plane with \(OA\) on a horizontal support.

  1. Find the coordinates of the centre of mass of triangle \(ABC\).

    [3]

  2. Find the complete range of \(h\) for which the lamina can remain in equilibrium on \(OA\). Include the toppling threshold.

    [4]

  3. At the toppling threshold, \(k=2/\sqrt3\). Find the coordinates of the triangular part’s centre of mass.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The centroid of a uniform triangular lamina is the mean of its vertex coordinates. Thus \[x_T=\frac{ka+(ka+h)+ka}{3}=ka+\frac h3,\qquad y_T=\frac{0+h+3a}{3}=a+\frac h3.\]

Part (b)

The rectangle has area \(3ka^2\), centre \((ka/2,3a/2)\); the triangle has area \(3ah/2\). The condition \(\bar x\le ka\) is equivalent to the first moment about the right-hand support endpoint being non-positive:

\[3ka^2\left(-\frac{ka}{2}\right)+\frac{3ah}{2}\left(\frac h3\right)\le0.\]

Hence \(h^2\le3k^2a^2\). All component centres have positive \(x\), so \(\bar x\ge0\) is automatic. With \(h\gt0\), the range is \(0\lt h\le\sqrt3ka\).

Part (c)

The threshold gives \(h=\sqrt3ka=2a\). Substitute this and \(k=2/\sqrt3\) into part (a) to obtain \(x_T=(2/\sqrt3+2/3)a\), \(y_T=5a/3\).
questions.hint_html: At incipient toppling, take moments about the edge of the supporting segment.

marking_criteria.description_html: Check the other endpoint and parameter domain.

questions.title: A quarter-disc attached to a rectangle
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform lamina consists of the rectangle \(-ka\le x\le0,\ 0\le y\le2a\) and the lower-right quarter of the disc of radius \(2a\) centred at \((0,2a)\). The two regions share the vertical radius \(0\le y\le2a\). Here \(k\gt0\). The lamina stands vertically on the rectangle's bottom edge, from \((-ka,0)\) to \((0,0)\). The quarter-disc touches that horizontal line only at \((0,0)\). You may use that the centre of mass of a quarter-disc of radius \(R\) is \(4R/(3\pi)\) from each bounding radius.

  1. Find the height of the centre of mass above the support.

    [4]

  2. Find \(k\) when the lamina is just about to topple about \((0,0)\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Areas are \(2ka^2\) and \(\pi a^2\). The rectangle centre is at height \(a\). The quarter-disc centre is at height \(2a-8a/(3\pi)\), since it is below its circle centre. Therefore \[\bar y=\frac{2ka^2(a)+\pi a^2\{2a-8a/(3\pi)\}}{(2k+\pi)a^2}=\frac{a(2k+2\pi-8/3)}{2k+\pi}.\]

Part (b)

At the threshold the horizontal first moment is zero: \[2ka^2\left(-\frac{ka}{2}\right)+\pi a^2\frac{8a}{3\pi}=0.\] Thus \(k^2=8/3\), and positivity gives \(k=2\sqrt6/3\).
questions.hint_html: The quarter-disc is below its centre; subtract its centroid offset when finding the height.

questions.title: Two corner cuts and a restricted base
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform square lamina has vertices \(A(0,0),B(4a,0),C(4a,4a),D(0,4a)\). Let \(E=(2a,0)\) and \(F=(4a-h,4a)\), where \(0\lt h\lt4a\). Remove triangles \(AED\) and \(BCF\). The remaining lamina \(EBFD\) is placed vertically with \(EB\) on a horizontal support.

  1. Find both coordinates of its centre of mass.

    [4]

  2. Find the allowed values of \(h\) for equilibrium, including limiting equilibrium.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The square area is \(16a^2\), at \((2a,2a)\). The removed triangles have areas \(4a^2\) and \(2ah\), with centroids \((2a/3,4a/3)\) and \((4a-h/3,8a/3)\). The remaining area is \(2a(6a-h)\).

Subtract the removed first moments:

\[\bar x=\frac{32a^3-4a^2(2a/3)-2ah(4a-h/3)}{2a(6a-h)}=\frac{h^2-12ah+44a^2}{3(6a-h)},\] \[\bar y=\frac{32a^3-4a^2(4a/3)-2ah(8a/3)}{2a(6a-h)}=\frac{8a(5a-h)}{3(6a-h)}.\]

Part (b)

The support runs from \(x=2a\) to \(x=4a\). The right bound is automatic since the lamina lies at \(x\le4a\). The other condition is \(\bar x\ge2a\). Since \(6a-h\gt0\),

\[h^2-12ah+44a^2\ge6a(6a-h)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(h-2a)(h-4a)\ge0.\]

Intersecting with \(0\lt h\lt4a\) gives \(0\lt h\le2a\). Equality is toppling about \(E\). The algebraic value \(h=4a\) is excluded by the stipulated domain.
questions.hint_html: Subtract mass moments as well as areas; the support is EB, not the whole original side AB.

questions.title: A mass at the tip of a bracket-shaped lamina
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform lamina of mass \(m\) is formed from the rectangle \(0\le x\le3a,\ 0\le y\le2a\) and the triangle with vertices \((3a,0),(3a,2a),(6a,a)\). A particle of mass \(km\) is attached at \((6a,a)\). The object stands in a vertical plane on the rectangle's lower edge, \(0\le x\le3a\).

  1. Find \(k\) if the object is on the point of toppling about \((3a,0)\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The rectangle and triangle have areas \(6a^2\) and \(3a^2\), so their masses are \(2m/3\) and \(m/3\). Their horizontal centres are \(3a/2\) and \(4a\). The lamina's horizontal centre is \[\bar x_L=\frac23\frac{3a}{2}+\frac13(4a)=\frac{7a}{3}.\]

At toppling the total centre is over \(x=3a\). Taking moments about that point,

\[m\left(3a-\frac{7a}{3}\right)=km(6a-3a),\] so \(2/3=3k\) and \(k=2/9\).
questions.hint_html: The mass m is the mass of both lamina regions together.

questions.title: A notch and an exact toppling threshold
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform right-triangular lamina has vertices \(C(0,0),A(0,8a),B(6a,0)\). Let \(D=(0,4a)\) and \(E=(x,0)\), where \(0\lt x\lt6a\). Triangle \(CDE\) is removed. The remaining lamina is placed vertically with \(EB\) on a horizontal support.

  1. Find the distance of its centre of mass from the line \(AC\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(x\) if the lamina is on the point of toppling about \(E\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The full triangle has area \(24a^2\) and horizontal centroid coordinate \(2a\). The removed triangle has area \(2ax\) and horizontal centroid coordinate \(x/3\). Thus \[\bar x=\frac{24a^2(2a)-2ax(x/3)}{24a^2-2ax}=\frac{72a^2-x^2}{3(12a-x)}.\] The denominator is positive throughout the stated domain.

Part (b)

At this threshold \(\bar x=x\). Hence \(72a^2-x^2=36ax-3x^2\), giving \[x^2-18ax+36a^2=0.\] The roots are \((9\pm3\sqrt5)a\). The plus root exceeds \(6a\), while \(0\lt9-3\sqrt5\lt6\). Therefore \(x=(9-3\sqrt5)a\).
questions.hint_html: Use the distance from AC as the horizontal coordinate, then compare it with the start of the supporting edge.

questions.title: A shortened supporting edge
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform triangle has vertices \(A(0,12a),B(0,0),C(8a,0)\). Let \(D=(x,0)\), with \(0\le x\lt8a\). Triangle \(ABD\) is removed; the remaining triangular lamina \(ADC\) stands vertically on \(DC\).

  1. Find the complete range of \(x\) for equilibrium, and describe the limiting configuration.

    [6]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(0\le x\le4a\); at \(x=4a\) toppling is impending about \(D\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The centroid of the remaining triangle is \[G=\left(\frac{x+8a}{3},4a\right).\] The horizontal support is the segment \(x\le X\le8a\). Its weight can be balanced by an upward reaction on that segment exactly when \[x\le\frac{x+8a}{3}\le8a.\] The first inequality gives \(x\le4a\), and the second gives \(x\le16a\), which is automatic in the domain. Hence \(0\le x\le4a\). At the upper endpoint the centre is vertically above \(D\), so the body is in limiting equilibrium about \(D\); beyond it the weight acts outside the base.

questions.title: Symmetric cuts, asymmetric support
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform square has vertices \(A(0,0),B(4a,0),C(4a,4a),D(0,4a)\). Let \(E=(4a-h,0)\) and \(F=(0,4a-h)\), where \(0\lt h\lt4a\). Remove triangles \(BCE\) and \(CDF\), leaving lamina \(AECF\).

  1. Find the coordinates of its centre of mass.

    [4]

  2. The lamina stands vertically on \(AE\). Find the values of \(h\) for equilibrium, including the threshold.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Reflection in \(y=x\) preserves the remaining region, so \(\bar x=\bar y\). The original area is \(16a^2\). Each removed triangle has area \(2ah\), and their horizontal centres are \(4a-h/3\) and \(4a/3\). Therefore \[\bar x=\frac{32a^3-2ah(4a-h/3)-2ah(4a/3)}{16a^2-4ah}=\frac{12a-h}{6}.\] The cancellation uses \(h\ne4a\), already ensured by the domain.

Part (b)

The supporting segment has endpoints \(0\) and \(4a-h\). Since \(\bar x\gt0\), the active condition is \[\frac{12a-h}{6}\le4a-h.\] Thus \(5h\le12a\). Combining this with \(0\lt h\lt4a\) gives \(0\lt h\le12a/5\). At \(h=12a/5\), the weight acts through \(E\); larger cuts cause toppling about \(E\).
questions.hint_html: Symmetry simplifies the centroid calculation, but it does not make every supporting edge equally safe.

questions.title: A square with one triangular corner removed
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform square has vertices \(C(0,0),B(0,12),A(12,12),D(12,0)\), in centimetres. Points \(E=(0,8)\) and \(F=(x,0)\), where \(0\lt x\lt12\), are marked and triangle \(CEF\) is removed.

  1. Find the coordinates of the remaining centre of mass.

    [4]

  2. The lamina stands vertically on \(FD\). Find the largest possible \(x\) for equilibrium.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The square has area \(144\) and centre \((6,6)\). The removed triangle has area \(4x\) and centre \((x/3,8/3)\). Hence \[\bar x=\frac{864-4x^2/3}{144-4x}=\frac{648-x^2}{3(36-x)},\qquad\bar y=\frac{864-32x/3}{144-4x}=\frac{648-8x}{3(36-x)}.\]

Part (b)

The support begins at horizontal coordinate \(x\). At the largest cut, \(\bar x=x\), so \[648-x^2=3x(36-x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x^2-54x+324=0.\] The two roots are \(27\pm9\sqrt5\). The plus root exceeds \(12\); the minus root is in \((0,12)\). Since \(\bar x-x\) is positive at \(x=0\) and changes sign at the first root, the maximum is \(27-9\sqrt5\) cm.
questions.hint_html: The horizontal support starts at F; a positive remaining area alone does not ensure equilibrium.

marking_criteria.description_html: Select and justify the maximum in the domain.

questions.title: Two possible cuts from a hanging trapezium
questions.prompt_html:
A square of side \(8a\) has vertices \(A(0,0),B(8a,0),C(8a,8a),D(0,8a)\). Let \(E=(h,8a)\) and \(F=(8a-h,0)\), where \(0\lt h\lt8a\). A uniform lamina occupies trapezium \(AFED\).

  1. Find the coordinates of its centre of mass.

    [4]

  2. The lamina is suspended from \(D\). The acute angle between \(DA\) and the downward vertical has tangent \(13/28\). Find the two possible values of \(h\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Split the trapezium along \(AE\). Triangle \(ADE\) has area \(4ah\) and centroid \((h/3,16a/3)\). Triangle \(AFE\) has area \(4a(8a-h)\) and centroid \((8a/3,8a/3)\). The total area is \(32a^2\).

The weighted coordinates are \[\bar x=\frac{4ah(h/3)+4a(8a-h)(8a/3)}{32a^2}=\frac{h^2-8ah+64a^2}{24a},\] \[\bar y=\frac{4ah(16a/3)+4a(8a-h)(8a/3)}{32a^2}=\frac{8a+h}{3}.\]

Part (b)

The horizontal and downward separations from \(D\) to \(G\) are \(\bar x\) and \(8a-\bar y=(16a-h)/3\). Thus \[\frac{h^2-8ah+64a^2}{8a(16a-h)}=\frac{13}{28}.\] Multiplying out and simplifying gives \(7h^2-30ah+32a^2=0\), or \((h-2a)(7h-16a)=0\). Both \(2a\) and \(16a/7\) lie strictly between \(0\) and \(8a\), so both geometries are valid.
questions.hint_html: Measure the vertical separation from D, not from the lower edge.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the correct vertical separation from D.

questions.title: Removing a corner before suspension
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform triangular lamina has vertices \(O(0,0),B(20a,0),C(0,15a)\). A point \(A=(x,0)\), where \(0\lt x\lt20a\), is chosen on \(OB\), and triangle \(OAC\) is removed.

  1. Find the distance of the remaining centre of mass from \(OC\).

    [3]

  2. The remaining lamina is suspended from \(C\). In equilibrium the acute angle between \(AB\) and the downward vertical has tangent \(6/5\). Find \(x\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The remaining region is exactly triangle \(ABC\), not a more complicated quadrilateral. Its horizontal centroid coordinate is the average of the three vertex coordinates: \[\bar x=\frac{x+20a+0}{3}=\frac{20a+x}{3}.\] Its vertical coordinate, needed next, is \(\bar y=5a\). Subtraction of mass moments gives the same result.

Part (b)

The vector from \(C\) to \(G\), measured in the original axes, has horizontal separation \((20a+x)/3\) and downward separation \(10a\). Since \(AB\) is originally horizontal, the tangent of its acute angle with \(CG\) is \[\frac{10a}{(20a+x)/3}=\frac65.\] Thus \(150a=120a+6x\), so \(x=5a\). This is within the side \(OB\). Using the reciprocal ratio would describe the angle with \(OC\), not with \(AB\).
questions.hint_html: The remaining lamina is itself a triangle. Check which edge is used in the angle condition.

questions.title: A similar triangular hole
questions.prompt_html:
An isosceles right-angled triangular lamina has vertices \(A(-3a,0),C(3a,0),B(0,3a)\). Points \(D\) on \(BA\) and \(E\) on \(BC\) satisfy \(BD/BA=BE/BC=1/k\), where \(k\gt1\). Triangle \(BDE\) is removed, leaving a uniform lamina symmetric about the \(y\)-axis.

  1. Find the distance of the centre of mass of the remaining lamina from the midpoint of \(AC\).

    [4]

  2. When suspended from \(A\), the acute angle between \(AC\) and the downward vertical has tangent \(2/9\). Find \(k\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The original triangle has area \(9a^2\) and centroid at height \(a\). The removed triangle has area \(9a^2/k^2\). Its centroid is at height \(3a-2a/k\), measured from \(AC\). By symmetry the remaining centre is on the \(y\)-axis, and \[\bar y=\frac{a-k^{-2}(3a-2a/k)}{1-k^{-2}}=\frac{a(k^3-3k+2)}{k(k^2-1)}=\frac{a(k^2+k-2)}{k(k+1)}.\] Cancellation is valid because \(k\gt1\).

Part (b)

The horizontal separation of \(G\) from \(A\) is \(3a\). Hence \(\bar y/(3a)=2/9\), giving \[\frac{k^2+k-2}{3k(k+1)}=\frac29.\] This simplifies to \(k^2+k-6=0\), so \(k=2\) or \(-3\). Only \(k=2\) satisfies the geometric requirement \(k\gt1\).
questions.hint_html: The removed mass scales as 1/k², not 1/k.

marking_criteria.description_html: Area ratio is the square of the scale factor.

questions.title: An asymmetric trapezium
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform trapezoidal lamina has vertices \(O(0,0),A(18,0),B(12,6),C(4,6)\), where coordinates are in centimetres.

  1. Find the \(x\)-coordinate of its centre of mass, giving an exact answer.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Split the trapezium into the rectangle \(4\le x\le12,\ 0\le y\le6\), a left right-triangle of base \(4\), and a right right-triangle of base \(6\). Their areas are \(48,12,18\), and their horizontal centres are \(8,8/3,14\), respectively. \[\bar x=\frac{48(8)+12(8/3)+18(14)}{48+12+18}=\frac{668}{78}=\frac{334}{39}\ \mathrm{cm}.\] This lies between the smallest and largest horizontal coordinates, as it must.
questions.hint_html: Split into a rectangle and two triangles; uniform area density makes area proportional to mass.

questions.title: A kite made from two triangles
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform kite-shaped lamina has vertices \(A(-4a,0),B(0,9a),C(10a,0),D(0,-9a)\).

  1. Find the distance of its centre of mass from \(BD\), stating which side of \(BD\) it lies on.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Triangles \(ABD\) and \(BCD\) have areas \(36a^2\) and \(90a^2\), with horizontal centres \(-4a/3\) and \(10a/3\). Hence \[\bar x=\frac{36a^2(-4a/3)+90a^2(10a/3)}{126a^2}=2a.\] The positive sign places the centre on the \(C\) side of \(BD\). Symmetry gives \(\bar y=0\).
questions.hint_html: Keep the centroid on the A side negative until the final distance is reported.
