questions.title: A loaded ladder: a parameter range
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform rod of length \(6a\) and weight \(W\) has its lower end \(A\) on rough horizontal ground and its upper end \(B\) against a smooth vertical wall. The rod makes an acute angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal. A small object of weight \(kW\) is fixed at distance \(4a\) from \(A\), where \(k\gt0\). The coefficient of friction at \(A\) is \(1/3\).

  1. Find the distance along the rod from \(A\) to the centre of mass of the rod and object.

    [4]

  2. Find the reaction at the wall and the frictional force at the ground. Deduce the condition on \(\theta\) for equilibrium.

    [4]

  3. If \(\tan\theta=7/4\), find all possible \(k\), and identify the limiting case.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The rod's centre is \(3a\) from \(A\). Weight is proportional to mass in uniform gravity, so first moments may be taken using weights: \[(1+k)W s=W(3a)+kW(4a).\] Thus \(s=a(3+4k)/(1+k)\), which lies between \(3a\) and \(4a\) for \(k\gt0\).

Part (b)

Moments about \(A\) give \[R_B(6a\sin\theta)=W(3a\cos\theta)+kW(4a\cos\theta).\] Hence \(R_B=(3+4k)W/(6\tan\theta)\). Horizontal equilibrium requires friction towards the wall with magnitude \(F_A=R_B\). Vertical equilibrium gives \(N_A=(1+k)W\). The inequality \(F_A\le N_A/3\) gives \(\tan\theta\ge(3+4k)/[2(1+k)]\).

Part (c)

Insert the angle into the condition: \[\frac74\ge\frac{3+4k}{2(1+k)}.\] As \(1+k\gt0\), this is \(7+7k\ge6+8k\), so \(k\le1\). Together with the positive-mass condition, \(0\lt k\le1\). Both contact reactions are positive. At \(k=1\) the friction reaches \(N_A/3\); for \(0\lt k\lt1\) it is below its limiting value.
questions.hint_html: For ordinary equilibrium use F ≤ μN. Equality is reserved for impending slip.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use a friction inequality, not automatic equality.

questions.title: A loaded rod with two rough contacts
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\) of length \(5a\) and weight \(W\) rests with \(A\) on rough horizontal ground and \(B\) against a rough vertical wall. The horizontal and vertical separations from \(A\) to \(B\) are \(3a\) and \(4a\). A particle of weight \(W/2\) is fixed at distance \(2a\) along the rod from \(A\). Both contacts are at limiting equilibrium, with \(A\) about to move away from the wall and \(B\) about to move down. The ground coefficient of friction is \(1/4\).

  1. Find both normal reactions and both frictional forces.

    [6]

  2. Find the coefficient of friction at the wall.

    [3]

  3. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant contact force at \(B\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(N_A=6W/5,\ R_B=3W/10,\ F_A=3W/10\) towards the wall, \(F_B=3W/10\) upwards.

(b)

\(\mu_B=1\).

(c)

\(3\sqrt2W/10\), at \(45^\circ\) above the horizontal away from the wall.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Friction at \(A\) acts towards the wall and friction at \(B\) acts upwards. Let \(N_A\) be the upward ground normal and \(R_B\) the horizontal wall normal. Then \[F_A=\frac14N_A,\qquad R_B=F_A,\qquad N_A+F_B=\frac32W.\] The rod centre and particle have horizontal distances \(3a/2\) and \(6a/5\) from \(A\). Taking moments about \(A\), \[4aR_B+3aF_B=\frac32aW+\frac12W\frac{6a}{5}=\frac{21}{10}aW.\] Substitute \(R_B=N_A/4\), \(F_B=3W/2-N_A\): \[N_A+\frac92W-3N_A=\frac{21}{10}W,\] so \(N_A=6W/5\), and the other three forces each have magnitude \(3W/10\). All assumed directions are confirmed.

Part (b)

Because the wall contact is also limiting, \[\mu_B=\frac{F_B}{R_B}=\frac{3W/10}{3W/10}=1.\] The ground normal must not be used in this ratio: each friction force has its own contact normal.

Part (c)

The wall force has equal horizontal and upward components, each \(3W/10\). Its magnitude is \[\sqrt{R_B^2+F_B^2}=\frac{3\sqrt2}{10}W.\] It is directed away from the wall and upwards, at \(45^\circ\) to the horizontal.
questions.hint_html: Both friction forces oppose the specified impending movements. Include the wall friction when taking moments.

questions.title: A rod against a rough wall
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\) has length \(6a\) and weight \(W\). Its end \(A\) touches a rough vertical wall; the rod extends upwards and away from the wall at angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal, with \(\tan\theta=1/2\). A light inextensible string of length \(4a\) joins the point \(C\), where \(AC=4a\), to a point \(D\) on the wall above \(A\). The rod is just about to slip down the wall.

  1. Find the string tension.

    [5]

  2. Find the coefficient of friction between rod and wall.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Triangle \(ACD\) is isosceles because \(AC=CD=4a\). Thus the string runs upwards towards the wall at angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal. With \(s=1/\sqrt5\), \(c=2/\sqrt5\), its components at \(C\) are \((-Tc,Ts)\).

The moment of the tension about \(A\) is \(8aTsc\). The rod weight has moment \(3aWc\). Therefore \[8aTsc=3aWc,\qquad T=\frac{3W}{8s}=\frac{3\sqrt5}{8}W.\]

Part (b)

At \(A\), the normal reaction acts away from the wall and friction acts upwards. Horizontal balance gives \(R=Tc=3W/4\). Vertical balance gives \(F=W-Ts=W-3W/8=5W/8\). Hence \[\mu=\frac FR=\frac{5W/8}{3W/4}=\frac56.\] Both forces are positive, so the assumed downward impending slip is consistent.
questions.hint_html: The equal rod segment and string length determine the cable angle; the wall reaction has two components.

questions.title: Moving a heavy load along a ladder
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\), length \(3a\) and weight \(W\), has \(A\) on rough horizontal ground and \(B\) against a smooth vertical wall. It makes an acute angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal. A particle of weight \(3W\) is initially attached at distance \(xa\) from \(A\), where \(0\lt x\lt3/2\).

  1. Find the wall reaction in terms of \(x,W\) and \(\theta\).

    [4]

  2. The particle is moved a distance \(a\) up the rod. The wall reaction doubles while \(\theta\) stays unchanged. Find \(x\).

    [3]

  3. The coefficient of friction at \(A\) is \(1/2\). If the second position is limiting equilibrium, find \(\tan\theta\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The horizontal moment arms of the rod weight and particle weight are \((3a/2)\cos\theta\) and \(xa\cos\theta\). The wall force has lever arm \(3a\sin\theta\). Thus \[3aR_B\sin\theta=W\frac{3a}{2}\cos\theta+3Wxa\cos\theta,\] so \(R_B=(1/2+x)W/\tan\theta\).

Part (b)

The reaction in the second position is \((3/2+x)W/\tan\theta\). Hence \(3/2+x=2(1/2+x)\), giving \(x=1/2\). The two load positions are \(a/2\) and \(3a/2\), both on the rod.

Part (c)

The ground normal supports the full weight, so \(N_A=4W\). At the limit, friction is \(2W\), and horizontal equilibrium makes the wall reaction \(2W\). With \(x=1/2\), the second reaction is \(2W/\tan\theta\). Hence \(2W/\tan\theta=2W\), giving \(\tan\theta=1\).
questions.hint_html: The total weight is unchanged when the particle moves, but its moment is not.

questions.title: A tied ladder with reversed friction
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\), length \(5a\) and weight \(W\), leans from rough horizontal ground at \(A\) to a smooth vertical wall at \(B\), with \(\tan\theta=2\). The foot of the wall is \(D\). A taut light rope joins \(D\) to \(C\) on the rod and is perpendicular to the rod. The rod is in equilibrium. The frictional force at \(A\) acts away from the wall and has magnitude one quarter of the normal reaction there.

  1. Find \(AC\).

    [2]

  2. Find the tension in the rope.

    [5]

  3. Find the two normal reactions and the magnitude of the frictional force.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The horizontal separation \(AD\) is \(5a\cos\theta\). Project \(AD\) onto the rod: \(AC=AD\cos\theta=5a\cos^2\theta\). Since \(\tan\theta=2\), \(\cos^2\theta=1/5\), so \(AC=a\).

Part (b)

Let \(s=2/\sqrt5\), \(c=1/\sqrt5\), and let the wall reaction be \(R\). The rope pulls towards \(D\), with components \((Ts,-Tc)\). Friction acts away from the wall as specified. With ground normal \(N=W+Tc\), horizontal balance gives \(R=Ts-N/4\).

Taking moments about \(A\), \[R(5as)=T(a)+W\frac{5a}{2}c.\] After division, \(R=(Tc^2+Wc/2)/s\). Combining with the force balance yields \(5T/(4\sqrt5)=W/2\), hence \(T=2\sqrt5W/5\).

Part (c)

With the tension found, \[N=W+Tc=W+\frac25W=\frac75W.\] Hence \(F=N/4=7W/20\), away from the wall. Horizontal equilibrium gives \(R=Ts-F=4W/5-7W/20=9W/20\). Both normals and the tension are positive, confirming the assumed contact configuration.
questions.hint_html: A taut rope can reverse the required friction direction. Use the specified force ratio, not the usual untied-ladder picture.

questions.title: Finding the load position at impending wall slip
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\), length \(8a\) and weight \(W\), touches a rough vertical wall at \(A\) and extends upwards away from it. The angle between rod and wall has tangent \(2\). A light inextensible string of length \(4a\) joins the midpoint \(C\) to a point \(D\) on the wall above \(A\). A particle of weight \(W\) is attached at \(E\), with \(AE=ka\) and \(4\lt k\lt8\). The wall coefficient of friction is \(1/4\), and the rod is about to slip down the wall.

  1. Find \(k\).

    [5]

  2. Find the magnitude of the frictional force.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let \(\phi\) be the rod angle above the horizontal; then \(\tan\phi=1/2\). Since \(AC=CD=4a\), the string makes angle \(\phi\) above the horizontal towards the wall. Moments about \(A\) give \[8aT\sin\phi\cos\phi=W(4+k)a\cos\phi,\] so \(T\sin\phi=(4+k)W/8\). The wall normal is \(R=T\cos\phi=(4+k)W/4\). Upward friction is \[F=2W-T\sin\phi=\frac{12-k}{8}W.\] At the limit, \((12-k)/8=(4+k)/16\), yielding \(k=20/3\). This lies in \((4,8)\).

Part (b)

Substitute \(k=20/3\) into \(F=(12-k)W/8\): \[F=\frac{12-20/3}{8}W=\frac23W.\] It acts upwards, opposing the specified downward slip.
questions.hint_html: The specified angle is with the wall; convert it before resolving vertically.

marking_criteria.description_html: Relate the wall angle to the horizontal angle.

questions.title: A suspended square tending to move upwards
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform square lamina \(ABCD\), side \(2a\) and weight \(W\), touches a rough vertical wall at \(B\). Side \(BA\) extends upwards to the right, making an acute angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal. The square lies below and to the right of \(BA\). A light string joins the midpoint \(E\) of \(AB\) to a point above \(B\) on the wall. The string is perpendicular to \(AB\), so it also makes angle \(\theta\) with the vertical. The coefficient of friction is \(1/3\); \(B\) is about to slip upwards.

  1. Find \(\tan\theta\).

    [8]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let \(s=\sin\theta\), \(c=\cos\theta\). Relative to \(B\), \(E=(ac,as)\) and the square centre is \(G=(a(c+s),a(s-c))\). The string force has components \((-Ts,Tc)\), so its moment about \(B\) is \(aT\). Balancing moments gives \(T=W(c+s)\).

The wall normal is \(N=Ts\). Because impending slip is upwards, friction acts downwards, with magnitude \(N/3\). Vertical balance is therefore \[Tc-\frac13Ts=W.\] Substituting \(T\) gives \((c+s)(c-s/3)=1\). Divide by \(c^2\) and set \(t=\tan\theta\): \[(1+t)(1-t/3)=1+t^2.\] This reduces to \(2t-4t^2=0\). The root \(t=0\) is excluded by the acute-angle assumption, so \(t=1/2\). Then \(T=3W/\sqrt5\), \(N=3W/5\), and downward friction \(W/5\), all positive and consistent.
questions.hint_html: Upward impending motion means downward friction. Do not impose the usual upward friction automatically.

marking_criteria.description_html: Correct centre and tension moment about B.

questions.title: A conical solid with a hemispherical cavity
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform solid cone has base radius \(4r\) and height \(8r\). A hemispherical cavity of radius \(2r\) is removed, with its flat face in the base plane of the cone and its curved surface inside the cone. The symmetry axes coincide. You may use that a uniform solid cone has its centre of mass one quarter of its height from its base, and a uniform solid hemisphere of radius \(R\) has its centre \(3R/8\) from its plane face.

  1. Find the height of the remaining centre of mass above the base.

    [4]

  2. The object is placed with its base on an inclined plane sufficiently rough to prevent sliding. Find the angle \(\alpha\) at incipient toppling.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Using a common volume unit \(\pi r^3/3\), the original cone has mass proportional to \(128\), and the removed hemisphere has mass proportional to \(16\). Their centres are \(2r\) and \(3r/4\) above the base. Therefore \[\bar z=\frac{128(2r)-16(3r/4)}{128-16}=\frac{244r}{112}=\frac{61r}{28}.\] The subtraction is of both mass and first moment; the cavity is not an added component.

Part (b)

The centre lies on the symmetry axis. At toppling its vertical projection reaches the downhill rim of radius \(4r\). Thus \[\bar z\tan\alpha=4r.\] With \(\bar z=61r/28\), \(\tan\alpha=112/61\). The acute inclination is \(\tan^{-1}(112/61)\).
questions.hint_html: Use volume as a mass weight, then project the remaining centre onto the inclined base.

questions.title: A blind cylindrical bore with two possible depths
questions.prompt_html:
A coaxial cylindrical hole of radius \(a/2\) and depth \(kh\), where \(0\lt k\lt1\), is bored downwards from the top of a uniform solid cylinder of radius \(a\) and height \(h\). Let \(AB\) be a diameter of the top face. The remaining body is suspended freely from the rim point \(A\).

  1. Find the distance \(d\) of the remaining centre of mass below the top face.

    [4]

  2. Given \(h=3a\), find all possible \(k\) for which the acute angle between \(AB\) and the downward vertical has tangent \(8/5\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Use \(\rho\pi a^2h\) as a mass unit. The full cylinder has mass \(1\), centre \(h/2\) below the top. The removed cylinder has mass \(k/4\), centre \(kh/2\) below the top. Hence \[d=\frac{h/2-(k/4)(kh/2)}{1-k/4}=\frac{h(4-k^2)}{2(4-k)}.\] By axial symmetry there is no horizontal offset from the cylinder axis.

Part (b)

From the suspension point to the centre there is an axial separation \(d\) and a radial separation \(a\). Since \(AB\) lies in the top face, \(\tan\theta=d/a\). Therefore \[\frac{3(4-k^2)}{2(4-k)}=\frac85.\] This gives \(15k^2-16k+4=0\), or \((5k-2)(3k-2)=0\). Both \(2/5\) and \(2/3\) lie in \((0,1)\), so both bore depths are possible.
questions.hint_html: Measure all centre positions from the same top plane before subtracting.

marking_criteria.description_html: Check both roots against the cavity domain.

questions.title: An eccentric cylinder on a hemisphere
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform solid hemisphere of radius \(3a\) occupies the region below its horizontal plane face. In a vertical cross-section, the centre of this face is \(C=(3a,0)\) and its left rim point is \(O=(0,0)\). A uniform solid cylinder of radius \(a\) and height \(d\) is attached above the face, with its axis through \((a,0)\). Both solids have the same density. You may use that a solid hemisphere's centre is \(3R/8\) below its plane face. The body rests on its curved hemispherical surface on a rough plane rising to the left, at an angle \(\theta\) with \(\sin\theta=1/5\). In the stated equilibrium orientation, \(OC\) is horizontal. Sliding is prevented.

  1. Find the coordinates of its centre of mass, relative to \(O\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(d\) in terms of \(a\). You are not required to determine whether the equilibrium is stable.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The hemisphere and cylinder volumes are \(18\pi a^3\) and \(\pi a^2d\). Their centres are \((3a,-9a/8)\) and \((a,d/2)\). Cancelling the common density and \(\pi a^2\), \[\bar x=\frac{18a(3a)+d(a)}{18a+d}=\frac{a(54a+d)}{18a+d},\] \[\bar y=\frac{18a(-9a/8)+d(d/2)}{18a+d}=\frac{2d^2-81a^2}{4(18a+d)}.\]

Part (b)

With only weight and the contact force acting, their lines of action must coincide. The contact point lies vertically below \(G\). For a plane rising leftwards, the contact point is \(3a\sin\theta\) to the left of \(C\). Its horizontal coordinate is therefore \(3a-3a/5=12a/5\).

Set \(\bar x=12a/5\): \[\frac{54a+d}{18a+d}=\frac{12}{5}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad270a+5d=216a+12d.\] Thus \(d=54a/7\). This is positive. The contact resultant must be vertical, so preventing slip requires at least \(\mu\ge\tan\theta=1/(2\sqrt6)\); sufficient friction was assumed. This moment condition asserts equilibrium, not stability.
questions.hint_html: The normal radius locates the contact point; the resultant contact force need not be normal to a rough plane.

marking_criteria.description_html: Vertical line through the centre and contact.

questions.title: A closed thin cylinder with a hemispherical cap
questions.prompt_html:
A thin uniform closed cylindrical shell, radius \(a\) and height \(h\), is joined to a thin hemispherical shell of radius \(a\) along the top rim. The hemisphere bulges upwards. Both are made of material with the same mass per unit area. Both circular end faces of the closed cylinder remain present, including the top face under the cap. You may use that the centre of a hemispherical shell is \(a/2\) from its plane face. Here \(h\gt0\).

  1. Find the height of the combined centre of mass above the lower face of the cylinder.

    [4]

  2. The lower circular face rests on a plane with inclination \(\tan\theta=2/3\). Friction is sufficient to prevent sliding. Find the range of \(h\) for equilibrium, including the toppling threshold.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The cylinder's surface area is \(2\pi ah+2\pi a^2=2\pi a(h+a)\), with centre at \(h/2\). The hemisphere has area \(2\pi a^2\), with centre at \(h+a/2\). Thus \[\bar z=\frac{2\pi a(h+a)(h/2)+2\pi a^2(h+a/2)}{2\pi a(h+2a)}=\frac{h^2+3ah+a^2}{2(h+2a)}.\] Using solid volumes here would model a different object.

Part (b)

The centre lies on the cylinder axis. No toppling requires \(\bar z\tan\theta\le a\), so \(\bar z\le3a/2\). Therefore \[h^2+3ah+a^2\le3a(h+2a)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h^2\le5a^2.\] Since \(h\gt0\), the range is \(0\lt h\le\sqrt5a\). Equality corresponds to the vertical weight line reaching the downhill rim.
questions.hint_html: This is a surface-density problem; the cylinder has two end discs as well as its curved surface.

questions.title: A cone on a cylinder: recovering the height ratio
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform solid cylinder has radius \(r\) and height \(h\). A uniform solid cone of the same material, with radius \(r\) and height \(kh\), is attached on top, with coincident axes and coincident joining faces. Here \(k\gt0\). You may use that the centre of a solid cone is one quarter of its height above its base.

  1. Find the height of the combined centre of mass above the lower circular face.

    [4]

  2. Now \(r=h\). With the lower face on a sufficiently rough plane, toppling begins when \(\tan\theta=10/9\). Find \(k\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Taking the cylinder mass as a unit, the cone mass is \(k/3\). Their centres are at \(h/2\) and \(h+kh/4\). Hence \[\bar z=\frac{h/2+(k/3)(h+kh/4)}{1+k/3}=\frac{h(k^2+4k+6)}{4(k+3)}.\]

Part (b)

At the threshold \(\bar z\tan\theta=r=h\), so \(\bar z=9h/10\). Thus \[\frac{k^2+4k+6}{4(k+3)}=\frac9{10}.\] This simplifies to \(5k^2+2k-24=0=(k-2)(5k+12)\). The negative root is inadmissible, leaving \(k=2\).
questions.hint_html: Use volumes for the mass ratio, then discard any negative cone height.

marking_criteria.description_html: Centre heights relative to a common base.

questions.title: A bore inside a hemisphere
questions.prompt_html:
A coaxial cylindrical cavity of radius \(a\) and depth \(ka\) is removed from a uniform solid hemisphere of radius \(2a\). The cavity opens at the hemisphere's plane face and extends into the solid. To keep it wholly inside the hemisphere, assume \(0\lt k\le\sqrt3\). Let \(AB\) be a diameter of the plane face. You may use that the original hemisphere's centre is \(3a/4\) below this face.

  1. Find the distance \(d\) of the remaining centre of mass below the plane face.

    [4]

  2. The body hangs freely from \(A\). The acute angle between \(AB\) and the downward vertical has tangent \(21/52\). Find all possible \(k\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

In units \(\pi a^3/3\), the full and removed volumes are \(16\) and \(3k\). Their centres are at depths \(3a/4\) and \(ka/2\). Hence \[d=\frac{16(3a/4)-3k(ka/2)}{16-3k}=\frac{3a(8-k^2)}{2(16-3k)}.\] The denominator and numerator are positive on the given domain. The cavity bound follows from \(a^2+(ka)^2\le(2a)^2\).

Part (b)

The radial distance from \(A\) to the symmetry axis is \(2a\). Therefore \(\tan\theta=d/(2a)\), so \[\frac{3(8-k^2)}{4(16-3k)}=\frac{21}{52}.\] Simplification gives \(13k^2-21k+8=0=(k-1)(13k-8)\). Both \(1\) and \(8/13\) are positive and at most \(\sqrt3\), so both cavity depths are geometrically possible.
questions.hint_html: An algebraic depth is not valid unless the cylindrical cavity fits inside the hemisphere.

questions.title: Locating the centre within one component
questions.prompt_html:
A solid cone of radius \(3r\) and height \(6r\) is joined at its base to a solid cylinder of radius \(kr\) and height \(4r\), where \(0\lt k\lt3\). Their axes coincide and their densities are equal. Measure axial distance \(z\) from the cone's vertex towards the cylinder. A point \(C\) is on the circumference of the cone's base. You may use that a solid cone's centre is three quarters of its height from its vertex.

  1. Find the axial position of the centre of mass.

    [4]

  2. The centre of mass lies inside the cylinder. When the object hangs from \(C\), the acute angle between the base diameter through \(C\) and the downward vertical has tangent \(1/6\). Find \(k\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The cone and cylinder volumes, in units \(\pi r^3\), are \(18\) and \(4k^2\). Their centres are at \(9r/2\) and \(8r\). Thus \[\bar z=\frac{18(9r/2)+4k^2(8r)}{18+4k^2}=\frac{r(81+32k^2)}{18+4k^2}.\]

Part (b)

The centre lies beyond the joining plane, so \(\bar z\gt6r\). The diameter direction is radial and the suspension radius is \(3r\); hence \[\frac{\bar z-6r}{3r}=\frac16,\qquad\bar z=\frac{13r}{2}.\] Substituting in part (a) gives \(81+32k^2=117+26k^2\), so \(k^2=6\). The positive root \(\sqrt6\) is less than \(3\). Also \(6r\lt13r/2\lt10r\), confirming that the centre lies within the cylinder. The stated location fixes the otherwise ambiguous sign of \(\bar z-6r\).
questions.hint_html: The phrase “inside the cylinder” determines the sign in the suspension geometry.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the stated component to choose the sign.

questions.title: Suspending a conical frustum
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform conical frustum has height \(h\), lower radius \(4r\) and upper radius \(r\). It is formed by removing a smaller similar cone from a larger cone. Let \(AB\) be a diameter of the lower face. You may use that the centre of a solid cone is one quarter of its height from its base.

  1. Find the distance of the frustum’s centre of mass above its lower face.

    [4]

  2. The frustum hangs freely from \(B\). If \(h=28r/3\), find the tangent of the acute angle between \(AB\) and the downward vertical.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Similarity gives the original cone height \(4h/3\) and the removed cone height \(h/3\). Their volumes are in the ratio \(64:1\). Relative to the lower face, their centres are \(h/3\) and \(h+h/12=13h/12\). Thus \[\bar z=\frac{64(h/3)-13h/12}{63}=\frac{9h}{28}.\]

Part (b)

The axial separation is \(\bar z=9(28r/3)/28=3r\); the radial separation from \(B\) to the axis is \(4r\). Therefore \(\tan\theta=3r/(4r)=3/4\).
questions.hint_html: The removed cone centre must be located relative to the lower face, not its own base.

questions.title: Resting on a cone generator
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform solid cone has height \(3r\) and base radius \(4r\). A uniform solid cylinder of radius \(4r\) and height \(3r\), made of the same material, is attached to the cone's base with coincident axes. You may use that the centre of a uniform solid cone is three quarters of its height from its vertex. The assembly is placed with one complete straight generator of the cone in contact with a horizontal plane.

  1. Find the distance of the centre of mass from the free circular end of the cylinder.

    [4]

  2. Show that equilibrium is possible in this position by locating the vertical projection of the centre of mass on the contacting generator.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(33r/16\).

(b)

The projection is \(189r/80\) from the vertex, strictly between \(0\) and \(5r\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Measure along the axis from the cone vertex \(V\). The cone and cylinder volumes are \(16\pi r^3\) and \(48\pi r^3\), and their centres are \(9r/4\) and \(9r/2\) from \(V\). Hence \[VG=\frac{16(9r/4)+48(9r/2)}{64}=\frac{63r}{16}.\] The free cylinder end is \(6r\) from \(V\), so the required distance is \(6r-63r/16=33r/16\).

Part (b)

The generator has length \(\sqrt{(3r)^2+(4r)^2}=5r\). If its angle with the axis is \(\beta\), then \(\cos\beta=3/5\). Since the generator is horizontal, the vertical projection of \(G\) lies at distance \[VG\cos\beta=\frac{63r}{16}\frac35=\frac{189r}{80}\] from the vertex along that generator. This is strictly between its endpoints \(0\) and \(5r\). An upward support resultant through this point balances the weight with zero net moment. No friction is required on a horizontal plane. This establishes possible equilibrium, not a statement about stability against every perturbation.
questions.hint_html: The relevant base is the contacting generator, not the cone’s circular face.

marking_criteria.description_html: Convert to distance from the requested end.

questions.title: A hinged rod with a perpendicular elastic string
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\), length \(5a\) and weight \(W\), is hinged to a vertical wall at \(A=(0,0)\). It is held with \(B=(4a,3a)\). A particle of weight \(W/2\) is fixed at \(B\). A light elastic string joins \(C\), the point on the rod with \(AC=3a\), to \(D=(0,5a)\) on the wall.

  1. Show that the string is perpendicular to the rod and find its tension.

    [3]

  2. Find the magnitude and direction of the hinge reaction.

    [4]

  3. The natural length of the string is \(3a\). Find its modulus of elasticity.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(CD=4a,\quad T=4W/3\).

(b)

\(R=\sqrt{745}W/30\), at \(\tan^{-1}(13/24)\) above the horizontal away from the wall.

(c)

\(\lambda=4W\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Since the rod has direction ratios \(4:3\), \(C=(12a/5,9a/5)\). From \(C\) to \(D\), the horizontal and vertical displacements are \(-12a/5\) and \(16a/5\), so \(CD=4a\). The string has direction ratios \(-3:4\), perpendicular to \(4:3\).

Its moment about \(A\) is therefore \(3aT\). The downward loads have moment \(W(2a)+(W/2)(4a)=4Wa\). Hence \(3aT=4Wa\), giving \(T=4W/3\).

Part (b)

The cable components are \(-3T/5\) and \(4T/5\). Thus the hinge components are \[H=\frac35T=\frac45W,\qquad V=\frac32W-\frac45T=\frac{13}{30}W.\] Both are positive in the rightward and upward directions. Consequently \[R=W\sqrt{\left(\frac45\right)^2+\left(\frac{13}{30}\right)^2}=\frac{\sqrt{745}}{30}W,\qquad\tan\phi=\frac{V}{H}=\frac{13}{24}.\]

Part (c)

The actual length is \(4a\), so the extension is \(a\), not \(4a\). Hooke's law gives \[T=\frac{\lambda e}{l}=\frac{\lambda a}{3a}=\frac{\lambda}{3}.\] Using \(T=4W/3\) gives \(\lambda=4W\). The extension and tension are positive, so the string is taut as assumed.
questions.hint_html: Take moments about the hinge, then resolve forces; use extension rather than actual length in Hooke’s law.

questions.title: A downward arm with an elastic tie
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\), length \(5a\) and weight \(W\), is hinged at \(A=(0,0)\) and held with \(B=(3a,-4a)\). A light elastic string joins \(B\) to \(O=(9a,4a)\). Its natural length is \(8a\). The rod and string lie in one vertical plane.

  1. Find the string tension.

    [3]

  2. Find the modulus of elasticity.

    [3]

  3. Find the angle and direction of the hinge force relative to the horizontal.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(T=5W/16\).

(b)

\(\lambda=5W/4\).

(c)

\(\tan^{-1}4\) above the horizontal towards the left.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The string has displacement \((6a,8a)\) from \(B\), so its length is \(10a\), and its force components are \(3T/5\) rightwards and \(4T/5\) upwards. Their total anticlockwise moment about \(A\) is \[(3a)\frac{4T}{5}+(4a)\frac{3T}{5}=\frac{24aT}{5}.\] The rod weight acts at horizontal distance \(3a/2\). Equating moments gives \(24aT/5=3aW/2\), hence \(T=5W/16\).

Part (b)

The extension is \(10a-8a=2a\). Thus \(T=\lambda(2a)/(8a)=\lambda/4\). With \(T=5W/16\), the modulus is \(\lambda=5W/4\).

Part (c)

The hinge must oppose the rightward cable component, so \(H=-3T/5=-3W/16\). Its vertical component is \(V=W-4T/5=3W/4\). Thus the force points upwards and leftwards. Relative to the leftward horizontal, \[\tan\phi=\frac{3W/4}{3W/16}=4,\] so \(\phi=\tan^{-1}4\). Stating only an unsigned tangent would not identify the correct direction.
questions.hint_html: Because B is below A, both components of the cable tension have moments in the same sense.

questions.title: A hinged rod attached to a sliding ring
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\), length \(5a\) and weight \(2W\), is hinged to a wall at \(A=(0,0)\) and held with \(B=(4a,3a)\). A ring of weight \(W\) is at \(P=(a,7a)\) on a rough horizontal wire through \(Q=(0,7a)\). A light elastic string joins \(B\) to \(P\), and has natural length \(4a\). The ring is in limiting equilibrium. All forces and lengths are in the same vertical plane.

  1. Find the string tension.

    [3]

  2. Find the coefficient of friction between ring and wire.

    [2]

  3. Find the magnitude of the hinge reaction on the rod.

    [3]

  4. Find the modulus of elasticity of the string.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The string displacement from \(B\) is \((-3a,4a)\), so its length is \(5a\). It is perpendicular to the rod direction \((4,3)\). Moments about the hinge give \(5aT=2W(2a)\), hence \(T=4W/5\).

Part (b)

On the ring, tension acts towards \(B\), with components \(3T/5\) rightwards and \(4T/5\) downwards. Therefore friction is \(12W/25\) leftwards and the wire normal is \(W+16W/25=41W/25\) upwards. Thus \(\mu=(12/25)/(41/25)=12/41\).

Part (c)

On the rod, the string pulls leftwards and upwards. The hinge components are therefore \[H=\frac35T=\frac{12}{25}W,\qquad V=2W-\frac45T=\frac{34}{25}W.\] Consequently \(R=W\sqrt{12^2+34^2}/25=2\sqrt{13}W/5\).

Part (d)

The string's extension is \(5a-4a=a\). Hooke's law gives \(T=\lambda/4\), so \(\lambda=4T=16W/5\). The string is stretched, as required.
questions.hint_html: Draw separate force diagrams for the rod and the ring; the string forces have opposite directions.

questions.title: A square supported at one vertex and one peg
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform square lamina has side \(4a\) and weight \(W\). Its vertex \(B\) rests on rough horizontal ground. The side \(BA\) runs upwards to the left and makes an acute angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal, with \(\tan\theta=1/2\). The square lies to the upper-right of this side. A smooth peg touches \(BA\) at \(E\), where \(BE=3a\), and pushes perpendicular to \(BA\), upwards and to the right. The lamina is in a vertical plane.

  1. Find the normal reaction \(R\) at the peg, the normal reaction \(N\) at the ground, and the friction at \(B\).

    [5]

  2. Find the coefficient of friction if the lamina is just about to slip.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Write \(s=\sin\theta=1/\sqrt5\), \(c=\cos\theta=2/\sqrt5\). Relative to \(B\), the centre of mass has horizontal coordinate \(2a(s-c)\). The peg reaction has components \((Rs,Rc)\). Its clockwise moment about \(B\) is \(3aR\), while the weight gives anticlockwise moment \(2aW(c-s)\). Thus \[3aR=2aW(c-s),\qquad R=\frac{2W}{3\sqrt5}.\] Vertical balance gives \(N=W-Rc=11W/15\). Horizontal balance requires friction \(Rs=2W/15\) to the left. All normal reactions are positive.

Part (b)

At limiting equilibrium \(F=\mu N\). Therefore \[\mu=\frac{2W/15}{11W/15}=\frac2{11}.\] The peg is smooth, so no tangential force is included there. The single friction force is at \(B\).
questions.hint_html: The square’s centre is displaced both along and perpendicular to the supported side.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use limiting friction at the correct contact.

questions.title: A movable smooth peg
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform rod \(AB\), length \(8a\) and weight \(W\), rests with \(A\) on rough horizontal ground. It extends upwards to the right with \(\tan\theta=3/4\). A smooth peg touches the rod at \(C\), where \(AC=x\), and pushes perpendicular to the rod, upwards and to the left. The coefficient of friction at \(A\) is \(\mu\gt0\). The rod is in limiting equilibrium, with \(0\lt x\le8a\).

  1. Express \(x\) in terms of \(a\) and \(\mu\).

    [4]

  2. Deduce a lower bound for \(\mu\).

    [3]

  3. If \(x=4a\), find \(\mu\) and the magnitude of the resultant contact force at \(A\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let the peg reaction be \(R\). Moment balance about \(A\) gives \(Rx=4aW\cos\theta\). Thus \(R=16aW/(5x)\). The ground forces are \[F=R\sin\theta=\frac{48aW}{25x},\qquad N=W-R\cos\theta=W\left(1-\frac{64a}{25x}\right).\] At limiting equilibrium \(F=\mu N\), so \(48a=\mu(25x-64a)\). Hence \(x=a(64+48/\mu)/25\).

Part (b)

The peg must lie on the rod, so \(x\le8a\). Substitute the result from part (a): \(64+48/\mu\le200\). Since \(\mu\gt0\), this gives \(\mu\ge48/136=6/17\). The formula also gives \(x\gt64a/25\), so the ground normal reaction is positive.

Part (c)

At \(x=4a\), the peg reaction is \(4W/5\). Therefore \(F=12W/25\) and \(N=9W/25\). Thus \[\mu=\frac{12}{9}=\frac43,\qquad R_A=\sqrt{F^2+N^2}=\frac{15W}{25}=\frac35W.\] The ground resultant acts upwards and to the right.
questions.hint_html: The peg position is restricted by the length of the rod, and the ground normal must stay non-negative.

questions.title: A tangent rod and a fixed disc
questions.prompt_html:
A smooth disc of radius \(a\) is fixed with its centre at \((5a/3,a)\), relative to a vertical wall \(x=0\) and ground \(y=0\). A uniform rod \(AB\), length \(3a\) and weight \(W\), has \(A=(0,a)\), and lies along the upper tangent from \(A\) to the disc. A particle of weight \(kW\), where \(k\gt0\), is fixed at \(B\). The wall coefficient of friction is \(1/3\), and \(A\) is about to slip down.

  1. Find \(k\).

    [8]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let \(C\) be the contact point and \(R\) the disc reaction. In the right triangle formed by \(A\), the disc centre and \(C\), the hypotenuse is \(5a/3\) and the radius is \(a\). Therefore \(AC=4a/3\), and the rod angle has \(\sin\theta=3/5\), \(\cos\theta=4/5\). The normal force at \(C\) acts upwards and to the left, with components \((-3R/5,4R/5)\).

Moments about \(A\) give \[R\frac{4a}{3}=W\frac{3a}{2}\frac45+kW(3a)\frac45,\qquad R=\frac9{10}(1+2k)W.\] The wall normal is \(N=3R/5\). Since impending slip is downwards, friction is upwards and equals \(N/3=R/5\). Vertical equilibrium gives \[\frac45R+\frac15R=(1+k)W,\qquad R=(1+k)W.\] Combining, \(9+18k=10+10k\), so \(k=1/8\). Then \(R=9W/8\), \(N=27W/40\), and friction \(9W/40\), all consistent with the assumed contact directions.
questions.hint_html: The reaction at the smooth disc is perpendicular to the rod, not vertical.

questions.title: A ring held by a horizontal string
questions.prompt_html:
A thin uniform ring of radius \(a\) and weight \(W\) rests on a rough plane rising to the right at angle \(\alpha\), where \(\tan\alpha=2/3\). Its plane is vertical and contains a line of greatest slope. Let \(O\) be its centre and \(K\) the contact point. Point \(P\) on the ring is on the upslope side, with \(OP\) parallel to the plane. A horizontal light string joins \(P\) to a fixed point \(Q\) on the plane to its right. The system is in limiting equilibrium.

  1. Find the string tension.

    [4]

  2. Find the coefficient of friction.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Write \(s=\sin\alpha\), \(c=\cos\alpha\). Relative to \(K\), the centre is at horizontal coordinate \(-as\), and \(P\) is at height \(a(c+s)\). The reaction and friction at \(K\) have zero moment there. Moment balance gives \[Wa s=Ta(c+s),\qquad T=\frac{Ws}{c+s}.\] Since \(s=2/\sqrt{13}\) and \(c=3/\sqrt{13}\), \(T=2W/5\).

Part (b)

Let \(F\) be positive upslope. Resolving parallel and normal to the plane, \[F+T\cos\alpha=W\sin\alpha,\qquad N=W\cos\alpha+T\sin\alpha.\] Thus \(F=4W/(5\sqrt{13})\), positive upslope, and \(N=19W/(5\sqrt{13})\). At the limit \(\mu=F/N=4/19\).
questions.hint_html: Take moments about the contact point so both unknown contact components disappear.

questions.title: A right-angled bracket on a rough cylinder
questions.prompt_html:
Two identical uniform rods \(AB\) and \(BC\), each of length \(2a\) and weight \(W\), are rigidly joined at right angles at \(B\). They rest against a fixed rough cylinder of radius \(a\), with the midpoint \(D\) of \(AB\) and midpoint \(E\) of \(BC\) as the contact points. The bracket lies in a vertical plane perpendicular to the cylinder axis. The rod direction from \(A\) to \(B\) is \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\), with \(0\lt\theta\lt\pi/4\). Relative to the cylinder centre, \(D=(-a\sin\theta,a\cos\theta)\) and \(E=(a\cos\theta,a\sin\theta)\). Both contacts have coefficient of friction \(\mu\), with \(0\lt\mu\lt1\), and the bracket is about to slip clockwise. Normal reactions at \(D\) and \(E\) are \(R\) and \(N\).

  1. Show that \(R:N=(1+\mu):(1-\mu)\).

    [4]

  2. Given \(\mu=1/4\), find \(\tan\theta\), and check that the normal reactions are positive.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Put \(s=\sin\theta\), \(c=\cos\theta\). The outward normals at \(D\) and \(E\) have directions \((-s,c)\) and \((c,s)\). To oppose clockwise slipping, friction at \(D\) acts along \((-c,-s)\), and at \(E\) along \((-s,c)\). Resolving parallel to the two rods gives \[N-\mu R=2Ws,\qquad R+\mu N=2Wc.\] Taking moments about the cylinder centre, both friction moments are anticlockwise, while the combined weight moment is \(Wa(s-c)\). Hence \[\mu(R+N)=W(c-s).\] From the two force equations, \(2W(c-s)=(1+\mu)R-(1-\mu)N\). Substitute this into the moment equation and rearrange: \[(1-\mu)R=(1+\mu)N.\] This gives the required ratio.

Part (b)

The ratio becomes \(R/N=5/3\); write \(R=5q\), \(N=3q\). The force equations give \[2Ws=3q-\frac54q=\frac74q,\qquad2Wc=5q+\frac34q=\frac{23}{4}q.\] Divide to obtain \(\tan\theta=7/23\), which is in \((0,1)\). Also \(c\gt0\) gives \(q=8Wc/23\gt0\), so \(R,N\gt0\). Both specified contacts are physically admissible.
questions.hint_html: Use the whole rigid bracket. Friction at the two contacts has different directions but the same rotational sense about the cylinder centre.

marking_criteria.description_html: Eliminate the angle to obtain the ratio.
Substitute μ in the first force equation.
Check the angle interval and positive reactions.

questions.title: A loaded rod tangent to a smooth cylinder
questions.prompt_html:
A smooth cylinder of radius \(4a/3\) is fixed to a rough horizontal floor, with its axis horizontal. A uniform rod \(AB\), length \(6a\) and weight \(W\), rests with \(A\) on the floor and is tangent to the cylinder at \(C\), where \(AC=4a\). The rod rises to the right with \(\tan\theta=3/4\), and the cylinder reaction is upwards and to the left. A particle of weight \(kW\) is attached at \(B\). The coefficient of friction at \(A\) is \(1\), and the rod is about to slip.

  1. Find the cylinder reaction \(R\) in terms of \(k\) and \(W\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(k\), checking that the ground normal reaction is positive.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The reaction is perpendicular to the rod, so its moment arm about \(A\) is \(4a\). The rod weight acts \(3a\) along the rod and the particle at \(6a\). Therefore \[4aR=W(3a)\frac45+kW(6a)\frac45,\] which gives \(R=3(1+2k)W/5\).

Part (b)

The cylinder reaction has horizontal magnitude \(3R/5\) and upward component \(4R/5\). Thus friction at \(A\) acts to the right, with \[F=\frac{9(1+2k)}{25}W,\qquad N=(1+k)W-\frac{12(1+2k)}{25}W=\frac{13+k}{25}W.\] At limiting equilibrium with \(\mu=1\), \(F=N\), so \(9+18k=13+k\). Hence \(k=4/17\). Substitution gives \(N=F=9W/17\gt0\), and \(R=15W/17\gt0\), so no contact is lost.
questions.hint_html: Only the component of the cylinder reaction normal to the floor contributes to the ground normal balance.
